passage:
Playgroup note from Zeenat, Tuesday
Anand (2½) came to me at snack time, tugged my dupatta and said, "Water, please." That's new; last month he just cried at the jug. Later he tried to open the art cupboard. I said, "That one is for teachers," and he closed it and went back to the blocks. With the class rabbit he stroked its back with two fingers, the way we practised, and whispered "soft." I've asked his father to keep using "gentle hands" at home 🙂

qa.q: What did Anand say when he tugged Zeenat's dupatta?
qa.a: He said, "Water, please."

qa.q: What does Anand whispering "soft" to the rabbit suggest?
qa.a: He seemed calm and tender with it, enjoying the gentle touch and maybe proud of doing it the practised way.

qa.q: How could Anand's father support what Zeenat saw?
qa.a: Keep using the same words at home, like "gentle hands", and answer quickly when Anand asks for things in words.

qa.q: What would change if Zeenat had snapped at Anand for opening the cupboard?
qa.a: He might have felt scared or ashamed, and a calm limit would have been harder for him to accept.

grounding: Shows a toddler asking for a need in words, accepting a limit and touching an animal gently, noted by his carer.

passage: The new calf in their village shed had wobbly legs and a wet nose. Hemant, two, ran at it with both arms up, and it skittered back. His mother Reena caught his hand. "Slowly. Like this." She laid her palm flat on the calf's neck. Hemant copied her, very slowly, and the calf sniffed his fingers. He giggled. Then he turned and said, "Doodh, Amma." Reena laughed. "The calf's milk first, then yours."

qa.q: Where was the new calf?
qa.a: In the village shed.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt when the calf sniffed his fingers?
qa.a: He seemed delighted and a bit thrilled, giggling at being so close to the calf.

qa.q: What could Reena keep doing to teach Hemant to be gentle with animals?
qa.a: Show him the slow, flat-hand touch each time and stay beside him, so he can copy it.

qa.q: How might the calf's reaction change if Hemant keeps running at it?
qa.a: It would keep backing away, so he would miss the close, friendly moment he got by going slowly.

grounding: Shows a toddler learning to touch an animal gently and asking his mother for what he needs.

passage: It was the dusty harmattan season in Accra, and Kwame kept the windows shut. His daughter Elif, two, stood at the door and said, "Out, Daddy? Out?" "Not today, the air's too dusty," Kwame said. She pouted but let go of the handle. Instead she knelt by the sleeping cat and patted it with one careful hand, the way he'd shown her, then looked up at him, beaming.

qa.q: Why did Kwame keep the windows shut?
qa.a: It was the dusty harmattan season.

qa.q: What does Elif beaming up at Kwame suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud of patting the cat gently and wanted her father to see.

qa.q: How could Kwame respond when Elif accepts a "not today"?
qa.a: Thank her for listening and offer something she can do inside, so accepting the limit feels good.

qa.q: What is it like for Kwame when Elif pouts but lets go of the handle?
qa.a: He may feel sorry she can't go out, and glad she accepts his reason without a fight.

grounding: Shows a toddler asking for what she wants, accepting a parent's limit and being gentle with a pet.

passage: Monday: Keerthana, five, held up her picture book to show her brother Divyansh the tiger, but she held it facing herself. "See?" she said. He only saw the back cover. Thursday: she showed him again, stopped, and asked, "Can you see it?" When he said no, she turned the book round. The next Sunday, on a video call with Paati, she held her drawing right up to the camera. "Can you see my tiger now, Paati?"

qa.q: What picture did Keerthana want to show Divyansh?
qa.a: The tiger in her picture book.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have been surprised when Divyansh said no on Thursday?
qa.a: She was starting to realise he couldn't see what she saw, and may have felt puzzled before turning the book round.

qa.q: How could Divyansh help Keerthana keep learning this?
qa.a: Tell her what he can actually see, like "just the back cover", so she learns to check.

qa.q: What would change for Paati if Keerthana still held drawings facing herself?
qa.a: Paati would only see the back of the paper and miss the tiger entirely.

grounding: Shows a young child learning over a week that someone opposite her sees a different view of a book or picture.

passage: The platform at the small station was packed because the train was an hour late. Eshaan, six, sat on his father's shoulders. His cousin Arohi, four, stood below, squeezed between suitcases, and kept asking, "Is it coming? Is it coming?" Eshaan could see the headlight far down the track. He looked down at her and realised she could only see legs and bags. "Arohi, it's coming! It's a blue engine. It's getting bigger!"

qa.q: What colour was the engine?
qa.a: A blue engine.

qa.q: What was Eshaan thinking when he looked down at Arohi?
qa.a: He realised she could only see legs and bags, and he seemed to feel for her and want her to share the excitement.

qa.q: What else could the adults do to help Arohi in the crowd?
qa.a: Lift her up for a moment when it is safe, or keep telling her what is happening as Eshaan did.

qa.q: What is it like for Arohi on the crowded platform?
qa.a: It is probably frustrating and a little scary to see nothing but legs while everyone waits for the train.

grounding: Shows a child realising that someone standing lower in a crowd sees a very different scene from him.

passage: In the kindergarten in Nagpur, the toy farm sat on a table between Asif and Harsha. Their teacher pointed at the plastic cow. "Asif, what can Harsha see of the cow?" Asif, five, said, "Its face." Then he frowned, got up, and walked round to Harsha's chair. "Oh. You see its tail!" He went back to his side and giggled. "I see face, Harsha sees tail."

qa.q: Which animal did the teacher point at?
qa.a: The plastic cow.

qa.q: What does Asif's frown suggest before he walked round?
qa.a: He seemed unsure and curious, sensing his first answer might be wrong.

qa.q: What did the teacher's question do well, and what might come next?
qa.a: It pushed Asif to check another view himself; next the teacher could ask him to guess before he walks round.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the moment when Asif came round to that chair?
qa.a: Harsha might find it funny and feel noticed, since Asif came to see things from that side.

grounding: Shows a young child discovering that a classmate across the table sees a different side of the same toy.

passage: I'm Dolma, from next door. On Saturday I was in Imran's kitchen when he finished the last two biscuits from the round tin and put the lid back on. He's five. Then he whispered to me, grinning, "Abbu will open it and think there are biscuits!" He waited by the door for his father. When Abbu opened the tin and said, "Arre, empty?", Imran burst out laughing. I'm not sure what he felt, but he looked very pleased with himself.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Imran finish?
qa.a: The last two biscuits.

qa.q: What does Imran's grin and whisper suggest?
qa.a: He was excited and amused, because he knew his father would believe the tin was still full.

qa.q: How could Imran's father use this moment?
qa.a: Play along, then talk about it: "You knew I didn't know!", and remind him to tell when the biscuits run out.

qa.q: How does Dolma see Imran's reaction?
qa.a: Dolma thinks he looked very pleased with himself, but is careful not to claim to know what he felt.

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that his father will wrongly believe a tin still holds biscuits, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: While his cousin Bittu was in the bathroom, Aparna moved the toy cars from the shelf to the basket. "Where will Bittu look?" she asked. "In the basket," said Naveen, four, pointing. Wednesday: they played again. Naveen opened his mouth, stopped, and said, "Um… the shelf? No, basket." Saturday: when Bittu went out, Aparna moved the cars again. Naveen shouted, "The shelf! Because Bittu didn't see you!"

qa.q: Where did Aparna move the toy cars from and to?
qa.a: From the shelf to the basket.

qa.q: What does Naveen stopping and saying "Um" on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: He was unsure and torn between what he knew and what Bittu knew, as the idea was just forming.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen reach the answer by Saturday?
qa.a: Playing the same game on several days, so he could keep trying without being corrected harshly.

qa.q: What would change if Bittu had watched Aparna move the cars?
qa.a: Then the basket would be the right answer, because Bittu would know where the cars are.

grounding: Shows a child coming to understand over a week that his cousin will believe the cars are where he last saw them.

passage: The rain started just as school ended. Jyoti, five, stood under the gate's shelter with her big brother Kiran, who had brought the umbrella from home that morning without telling anyone. "Mumma will look by the door for the umbrella," Jyoti said, "but it isn't there. She'll think it's lost." "So?" said Kiran. "So she'll be worried," Jyoti said. "Call her." Kiran rang from the watchman's phone.

qa.q: Who had brought the umbrella from home that morning?
qa.a: Her big brother Kiran.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti want Kiran to call Mumma?
qa.a: She was worried Mumma would look by the door, not find it, and feel upset thinking it was lost.

qa.q: What could Kiran do next time he takes something from home?
qa.a: Tell someone before he leaves, so nobody is left looking for it.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel when Kiran calls?
qa.a: Relieved that the umbrella isn't lost and glad the children thought of her.

grounding: Shows a young child understanding that her mother will wrongly think the umbrella is by the door and may think it lost.

passage: It had rained for three days, so hide-and-seek had to happen inside the one-room flat. Last year Mohit used to hide with his head under a cushion and his legs sticking out. Now, at five, he squeezed behind the steel almirah and held his breath. "Where's Mohit?" called his Dada Shankar, looking under the bed on purpose. Mohit clapped a hand over his mouth to stop a giggle. Dada didn't know! He waited until Dada went the wrong way, then jumped out.

qa.q: Where did Mohit hide this time?
qa.a: Behind the steel almirah.

qa.q: Why did Mohit clap a hand over his mouth?
qa.a: He was excited and trying not to giggle, because he knew Dada didn't know where he was and wanted to keep the trick going.

qa.q: How can Dada Shankar keep the game fun in such a small space?
qa.a: Keep looking in the wrong places on purpose and act surprised, so Mohit enjoys fooling him.

qa.q: What is it like for Dada Shankar to play in the cramped flat?
qa.a: He probably enjoys pretending to be fooled, even with little room to move.

grounding: Shows a young child playfully hiding and realising his grandfather cannot know where he is.

passage: Chinmay, four, waited until his mother Aparna went to the balcony in their Pune flat. Then he hid one of her slippers inside the laundry basket. When she came back and looked around, he sat on the sofa with a very straight face. "Chinmay, have you seen my slipper?" "No," he said, then his lips started to shake. She searched under the table. He couldn't hold it and shrieked, "It's in the basket! I tricked you!"

qa.q: Where did Chinmay hide the slipper?
qa.a: Inside the laundry basket.

qa.q: How can you tell Chinmay felt it was hard to keep the trick going?
qa.a: His lips started to shake and he burst out with the answer, because he was bursting with excitement.

qa.q: How could Aparna respond to keep this kind of trick playful and honest?
qa.a: Laugh with him and name it as a game, "You tricked me!", while keeping it to fun hiding games.

qa.q: What might Aparna be thinking when he sits there with a very straight face?
qa.a: She may guess he's up to something and feel amused, playing along to let him enjoy it.

grounding: Shows a young child playing a light trick and discovering his mother doesn't know what he knows.

passage:
"Close your eyes, Dhruv," Ritu said. "Which hand has the toffee?"
Dhruv, four, opened them and pointed. "That one!"
Ritu opened her right hand. Empty. "Wrong!"
"Again!"
This time Ritu, six, hid both hands behind her back and swapped the toffee twice. "Which one?"
"That one. I saw it there before."
"But I moved it! You didn't see!" She opened the other hand.
Dhruv stared, then grinned. "My turn to trick you."

qa.q: Which hand did Ritu open first?
qa.a: Her right hand.

qa.q: What does Dhruv's grin suggest when he says "My turn to trick you"?
qa.a: He was amused rather than upset and eager to try the trick himself.

qa.q: How could a parent keep this game fair and fun for both?
qa.a: Let them take turns hiding and guessing, and give the toffee to share at the end.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu when Dhruv guesses wrong?
qa.a: She enjoys knowing something he doesn't and feels clever about her swap.

grounding: Shows young siblings playing a guessing trick and realising the other doesn't know where the toffee is.

passage:
Teacher's note, Nirmala, sand corner
Leela (5) and three others were at the sand tray for twenty minutes. Each made something different: Leela a "cake", the boy beside her a road. They chatted the whole time, "Mine has candles," "Mine has a truck," and swapped spades twice. When Leela needed the sieve, she asked for it and got it. Nobody tried to make one thing together. Tomorrow I'll put out one big tray and see what happens 🙂

qa.q: How long were the children at the sand tray?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt while chatting beside the others?
qa.a: She seemed happy and interested, enjoying the company while making her own cake.

qa.q: Why is Nirmala's one-big-tray idea a sensible next step?
qa.a: It gently invites the children to share space and maybe a shared idea, without forcing them.

qa.q: How might the boy making the road see his time at the sand tray?
qa.a: He probably enjoyed having someone to talk to and swap spades with while still doing his own thing.

grounding: Shows children playing side by side, talking and sharing tools, each on their own project, noted by a teacher.

passage: Behind the temple in their small town, Usha and Minakshi, both five, sat in the wet clay by the pond. Usha was making tiny pots. Minakshi was making snakes. "Mine is for water," Usha said. "Mine is a king snake," said Minakshi. When Usha's clay got dry, Minakshi pushed the water tin towards her without being asked. They didn't make anything together; they just kept talking, each with her own lump, until the aarti bell rang.

qa.q: What was Usha making?
qa.a: Tiny pots.

qa.q: What does Minakshi pushing the water tin towards Usha suggest?
qa.a: She felt friendly and caring towards Usha, happy to share even though they weren't working together.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby support this kind of play?
qa.a: Give them space and enough clay and water, and let them chat without insisting they build one thing together.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about playing with Minakshi?
qa.a: She likely feels comfortable and content, enjoying company without having to agree on one plan.

grounding: Shows two young girls playing side by side in clay, talking and sharing water without a shared goal.

passage: On a warm Saturday in a Toronto park, Abebe, five, was drawing a rocket in chalk on the path, his tongue between his teeth. Jin, who lived in the same building, knelt a metre away and drew a very large cat. "My rocket goes to the moon," said Abebe. "My cat eats fish," said Jin. They traded the blue chalk for the yellow, then traded back. When Jin's cat's tail reached Abebe's rocket, neither minded. They each kept drawing their own picture.

qa.q: What was Jin drawing?
qa.a: A very large cat.

qa.q: What might Abebe have felt when Jin's cat's tail reached his rocket?
qa.a: He seemed relaxed and content, not bothered, because they were happy playing side by side.

qa.q: What could a parent do to extend this play?
qa.a: Offer more chalk and ask each child about their picture, without pushing them to join the drawings.

qa.q: What would change if one child wanted to make a single big picture together?
qa.a: They would need to agree on a plan, turning it into a different, more cooperative kind of play.

grounding: Shows two young children drawing side by side, chatting and swapping chalk, each on their own picture.

passage: In the courtyard of their Pune housing colony, Ojas and Salma, both five, had one goal: a sand tower tall enough to reach the bottom of the slide. "You bring water, I pat," Salma said. Ojas ran back and forth with a cup. When one side slumped, they both stopped. "More water," Ojas said. "No, too much," said Salma. "Less!" They patted together, carefully. The tower touched the slide, and they jumped up and down, shouting.

qa.q: What was the tower supposed to reach?
qa.a: The bottom of the slide.

qa.q: What were Ojas and Salma feeling when the tower touched the slide?
qa.a: They were thrilled and proud of reaching their goal together.

qa.q: What helped them work as a team?
qa.a: Splitting the jobs, water and patting, and talking about what went wrong when one side slumped.

qa.q: How might Salma see Ojas as a partner?
qa.a: As someone who followed the plan and stayed to fix the problem, which made the tower possible.

grounding: Shows two young children working together towards one goal, a tall sand tower.

passage:
"We need a train long enough for all the animals," said Uday.
"Twelve boxes," said his brother Anirban, counting. "We only have eight."
"Ask Amma for the shoe boxes!"
"You tape, I'll push them together."
"Your tape is crooked."
"Then you tape and I'll hold."
Uday held; Anirban taped.
"Elephant goes in the last box, he's heavy."
"Last box. Okay."
When the train was done, they lined up every animal and pulled it round the room together, both hands on the string.

qa.q: How many boxes did they say they needed?
qa.a: Twelve boxes.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Anirban said his tape was crooked?
qa.a: He may have felt a little stung, but he stayed calm and willing, swapping jobs so the train could get finished.

qa.q: Which choice kept the building going, and why?
qa.a: Swapping roles when the tape went crooked, because it fixed the problem without a fight.

qa.q: What would change if one brother had insisted on doing everything alone?
qa.a: The train would take longer, and they would lose the fun of building it together.

grounding: Shows two young brothers planning and building a toy train together to fit all their animals.

passage:
Nursery note from Rukmini, Thursday
Charu (5) and two friends decided to build a bridge of blocks so the toy cars could cross the "river" (a blue cloth). Charu held the two ends steady with her hands while the others laid the long block across. It fell twice. The third time, Charu said, "Let's make the towers fatter," and they did. The bridge held. They cheered and drove every car across. I took a photo for the wall and asked them to explain it at circle time.

qa.q: What did the blue cloth stand for?
qa.a: The "river".

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when the bridge held on the third try?
qa.a: Probably proud and excited, since her idea of fatter towers worked.

qa.q: Why is asking them to explain it at circle time a good idea?
qa.a: It lets them put their teamwork into words and feel their shared effort was noticed.

qa.q: How might Charu's two friends see her part in the building?
qa.a: They might see her as the one with the good idea, while they did the placing, so the success felt shared.

grounding: Shows young children cooperating on a block bridge and solving a problem together, noted by their teacher.

passage: In a London flat after school, Hiroshi and his friend Jamal, both five, turned the coffee table into a restaurant. "I'm the chef," said Hiroshi. "No, I'm chef," said Jamal. They stared at each other. "You can be chef today," Hiroshi said slowly, "and I'm the waiter, and tomorrow we swap." Jamal agreed. Hiroshi took orders from two teddies on a notepad, and Jamal served invisible noodles in paper bowls.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi and Jamal turn the coffee table into?
qa.a: A restaurant.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi speak slowly when he suggested swapping?
qa.a: He was thinking it through, torn between wanting to be chef and wanting the game to carry on.

qa.q: What could a parent do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: Offer props like paper bowls and a notepad, and let the children sort out the roles themselves.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel about Hiroshi's offer?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved to be chef, and more willing to be the waiter tomorrow.

grounding: Shows two young children negotiating roles in a pretend restaurant so the story can continue.

passage: At the preschool's pretend clinic corner, Vishal, five, put on the toy stethoscope. "I'm the doctor." Siddharth lay on the mat. "I have a tummy ache." "No, you broke your leg," said Vishal. "Tummy ache," said Siddharth firmly. Vishal paused. "Okay. You have a tummy ache and a broken leg." Siddharth laughed. "Okay!" Vishal bandaged his leg with a scarf and listened to his tummy.

qa.q: What did Vishal put on?
qa.a: The toy stethoscope.

qa.q: What does Vishal's pause suggest before he changed the story?
qa.a: He was working out how to keep his idea and Siddharth's, maybe feeling torn about giving up the broken leg.

qa.q: How could a teacher support play like this?
qa.a: Stay nearby and let them bargain, stepping in only if one child keeps overruling the other.

qa.q: If you were Siddharth, how would you feel about Vishal's compromise?
qa.a: Pleased and listened to, since the tummy ache stayed in the story.

grounding: Shows young children bargaining over the story in a pretend clinic until both ideas fit.

passage: I'm Manoj, Eshaan's uncle. Last weekend Eshaan, who is six, and his cousins lined up chairs in the hall and turned them into a train to Goa. Eshaan wanted to be the driver, but so did his cousin. They argued for a minute, then Eshaan said, "You drive, I'm the ticket checker." He walked up and down, punching pretend tickets. Later he announced, "Next station, beach!" and everyone climbed off. I can't say how much it bothered him, but he kept playing.

qa.q: Where was the pretend train going?
qa.a: To Goa.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have felt when he gave up being the driver?
qa.a: Maybe a little disappointed, but he seemed content in his new role since he kept playing happily.

qa.q: What small step could Manoj take to make role swaps fairer?
qa.a: Suggest a turn system, so Eshaan gets to drive next time.

qa.q: How does Manoj see the argument over the driver?
qa.a: Manoj notices it passed quickly and that Eshaan found another role, but doesn't claim to know Eshaan's feelings.

grounding: Shows young cousins negotiating roles in a pretend train journey, seen by an uncle.

passage: At the preschool playground, only one swing was working. Yash, five, grabbed it just as Arohi reached it. "It's mine!" "I was first!" Arohi pulled the chain. Their teacher came over and crouched. "Two children, one swing. What can we do?" Yash kicked the sand. Arohi said, "Ten pushes each?" Yash thought, then nodded. After his ten, he got off and mumbled, "Sorry I grabbed." Arohi gave him an extra push on his next turn.

qa.q: How many swings were working?
qa.a: Only one swing was working.

qa.q: What does Yash kicking the sand suggest?
qa.a: He was frustrated and didn't want to give up the swing yet.

qa.q: What worked in the teacher's approach, and why?
qa.a: Asking the children to find a solution let Arohi suggest turns, so they owned the fair plan.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Yash says sorry?
qa.a: She may feel respected and friendly again, which is why she gives him an extra push.

grounding: Shows two young children resolving a fight over a swing by taking turns and apologising, with a teacher's light help.

passage: I'm Rajni, Lakshmi's big sister. Yesterday Lakshmi, who is five, and her friend both wanted the same doll. They pulled it between them until one arm popped off, and both of them went quiet. Lakshmi looked like she might cry. Then she said, "You hold her body, I hold her arm, and we fix her." They pushed the arm back together. Later I heard her say, "Sorry for pulling." I don't know if she meant it fully, but they played till dinner.

qa.q: What happened to the doll when they pulled it?
qa.a: One arm popped off.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi have felt when the arm came off?
qa.a: She likely felt shocked and upset, maybe guilty, since she looked close to crying.

qa.q: How could an adult help next time before the doll breaks?
qa.a: Suggest turns early, like a timer or "you first, then me", before pulling starts.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Lakshmi's apology?
qa.a: Rajni is not sure it was fully meant, but notices it helped them keep playing.

grounding: Shows young children moving from a tug-of-war over a doll to a joint fix and an apology, seen by an older sister.

passage: Tuesday: Sharmila and Ganga, both five, fought over the one purple crayon in their class, and Ganga snapped it in half. Both cried. Thursday: their teacher gave them a sand timer. "Two turns each," she said. They took turns, watching the sand run, and argued only once. The next Monday: when Ganga reached for the purple, she stopped. "Sorry about the broken one," she told Sharmila. "You go first."

qa.q: What did Ganga do to the purple crayon on Tuesday?
qa.a: She snapped it in half.

qa.q: What does Ganga stopping and apologising on Monday suggest?
qa.a: She felt sorry about the broken crayon and wanted things to be fair with Sharmila.

qa.q: Why did the sand timer help?
qa.a: It made turns clear and fair, so the girls didn't have to argue about who had it longer.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel when Ganga offers her the first turn?
qa.a: Surprised and pleased, and more willing to share in return.

grounding: Shows young children learning over a week to take turns and apologise after a crayon fight.

passage: On a grey autumn morning in Manchester, Emeka, five, sat on the bedroom floor with his mother Clara and a pile of clean socks. "Find the partners," Clara said. Emeka made a red pile, a blue pile and a black pile. Then he stopped. "Black big, black small," he said, splitting the black pile into Daddy's and his own. Clara raised her eyebrows. "Two ways at once! Clever."

qa.q: What piles did Emeka make first?
qa.a: A red pile, a blue pile and a black pile.

qa.q: How might Emeka have felt when Clara said "Clever"?
qa.a: He probably felt proud that she noticed his extra sorting by size.

qa.q: How could Clara build on this at home?
qa.a: Give him other things to sort, like spoons or toys, and ask him to find another way to group them.

qa.q: What would change if Clara had simply paired the socks herself?
qa.a: It would be quicker, but Emeka would miss the chance to practise sorting by colour and size.

grounding: Shows a young child sorting socks by colour and then by size.

passage: The preschool maths table had a bowl of buttons. "Can you sort them, Harish?" asked Yamini, his teacher. Harish, four, made two heaps: round and square. A tiny star-shaped button didn't fit either. He held it up, frowning. "This one has no family." "What could you do?" Yamini asked. He thought, then made a third heap: "Star family." He looked up at her with a big smile.

qa.q: What was in the bowl on the maths table?
qa.a: Buttons.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he held up the star-shaped button?
qa.a: He seemed puzzled and a bit stuck, since it didn't fit his two heaps.

qa.q: Which choice by Yamini helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking "What could you do?" instead of telling him, so he found the answer of a new group himself.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Harish's star family?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased that he worked out a new category on his own.

grounding: Shows a young child sorting buttons by shape and creating a new group for one that doesn't fit.

passage: I'm Rekha, and I sell vegetables beside Seema's mother's bangle stall at the weekly market. Seema is five. Last Thursday the bangles got mixed up in a box, and she sat on the mat sorting them without being asked. First all the red, then the green, then the gold. Then she lined each colour up from big to small. Her mother only smiled. I can't say what Seema was thinking, but she didn't look up once until it was done.

qa.q: What colours did Seema sort first?

"Hello? Hello, Papa?" Chandrika held a banana to her ear.
Vijay looked up from his newspaper. "Who's calling?"
"It's the doctor. For you." She held out the banana.
He took it. "Hello, doctor. Yes... yes... my daughter needs a bath? Okay."
"No! Doctor said ice cream!"
"Ah, sorry, bad line." He gave it back.
Chandrika, five, pressed buttons on the banana. "Now I'm calling Nani." Then she peeled it and ate the phone.

qa.q: What did Chandrika use as a phone?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's shout "Doctor said ice cream!" suggest?
qa.a: She was enjoying the game and felt cheeky, wanting to steer the pretend call her way.

qa.q: What small step could Vijay take to extend the pretend play?
qa.a: Keep playing along and let her lead, maybe asking what else the "phone" can do.

qa.a: He seems amused and happy to play along, adding jokes of his own.

grounding: Shows a young child using a banana as a pretend phone with her father joining in.

Nikita (4) held a birthday party for the teddies today. She stood a wooden block on its end on a plate and said, "Cake." Then she pushed three pencils into the playdough on top: "Candles." She blew them out and cut the block with a paper knife. When another child took a "slice", she said, "Say thank you!" I joined in and sang. Tomorrow I'll add some old boxes to the pretend corner.

qa.q: What did Nikita use as a cake?
qa.a: A wooden block stood on its end.

qa.q: What does Nikita saying "Say thank you!" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was fully caught up in the pretend party and felt proud of hosting it.

qa.q: Why is adding old boxes a good idea for the pretend corner?
qa.a: Open-ended objects let children decide what they stand for, which feeds this kind of play.

qa.q: How might the child who took a "slice" feel?
qa.a: Included and happy to be part of Nikita's pretend party.

grounding: Shows a young child using blocks and pencils to stand for a cake and candles in pretend play.

passage: In their village, Hrithik, five, had a stick he called Badal, his horse. He galloped it round the neem tree every evening. His older sister Seema laughed. "That's just a stick." Hrithik stopped, face red, and hugged the stick to his chest. "It's Badal!" Seema saw his face and changed her tone. "Sorry. Does Badal want water?" She put a leaf in front of it. Hrithik brightened and made Badal drink.

qa.q: What did Hrithik call his stick?
qa.a: He called it Badal, his horse.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's face go red when Seema laughed?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry that she mocked Badal, who was real to him in the game.

qa.q: What did Seema do to repair things?
qa.a: She said sorry and joined the pretend game by offering the horse water, which respected his idea.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had kept laughing?
qa.a: Hrithik might have stopped playing or stayed resentful towards her.

grounding: Shows a young child using a stick as a horse in pretend play and his hurt when an older sister dismisses it.
